Importing the data:

```{r}
library(e1071)
```

```{r}
train_data<-read.csv("../processed-data/football_train_data.csv")
test_data<-read.csv("../processed-data/football_test_data.csv")
```

**Pre-processing**

```{r}
# Pulling out the predictor variables from the outcome
predictors<-setdiff(names(train_data), "FTR")

# Checking which predictors have no missing variables
selected_predictors <- predictors[
    colSums(is.na(train_data[, predictors, drop = FALSE])) == 0
]

selected_predictors
```

That seems to be a problem - all predictors have at least one row with missing values

```{r}
which(is.na(train_data$AST))
```

I personally inspected this in the Excel file, it had N/A for almost all of the match statistics weirdly.
So removing it for now.

```{r}
train_data1<-train_data[-8808,]
```

Trying again:

```{r}
sum(colSums(is.na(train_data1[, predictors, drop = FALSE])) == 0)
```

Only 10 - I would have thought 12; all the match statistics (non-betting odds)
Looking at which were fine:

```{r}
selected_predictors1 <- predictors[
    colSums(is.na(train_data1[, predictors, drop = FALSE])) == 0
]
selected_predictors1
```

AF and HF are the only two missing. Investigating:

```{r}
which(is.na(train_data$AF))
which(is.na(train_data$HF))
```

So now we'll use:

```{r}
train_data_NB<-train_data[-c(8808,32940,32949),]
selected_predictors_NB<- predictors[
    colSums(is.na(train_data_NB[, predictors, drop = FALSE])) == 0
]
```

which should work:

```{r}
sum(colSums(is.na(train_data_NB[, predictors, drop = FALSE])) == 0)
selected_predictors_NB
```


```{r}
nrow(train_data_NB)
nrow(test_data)
```

Now onto fitting an SVM:

```{r}
# Making outcome into a factor variable:

train_data_NB$FTR<-factor(train_data_NB$FTR, levels=c("H", "D", "A"))
test_data$FTR<-factor(test_data$FTR, levels=c("H", "D", "A"))

svm_model_NB<-svm(FTR~., data=train_data_NB[, c("FTR", selected_predictors_NB)],
               kernel="radial", cost=1, gamma=1/length(predictors), scale=TRUE)

```

```{r}
svm_predictions_NB<-predict(svm_model_NB, newdata=test_data[, selected_predictors_NB, drop=FALSE])
```

```{r}
confusion_matrix_NB<-table(Actual=test_data$FTR, Predicted=svm_predictions_NB)
```

```{r}
confusion_matrix_NB
Accuracy_NB<-sum(diag(confusion_matrix_NB))/sum(confusion_matrix_NB)
Accuracy_NB
```

So we have an accuracy of 57.5% which is isn't great. It didn't seem to predict many draws at all.
In fact we can do:

```{r}
round(diag(prop.table(confusion_matrix_NB, margin=1))*100, 2)
```

to see the percentage of correctly classified outcomes for each of Home Win, Draw and Away Win.
As we can see the model had a lot of trouble getting the draws, but seemed good at Home Wins and reasonable for
Away wins.

We will see how much of a difference knowing the bookmakers opening odds (specifically Bet365) can help it.
Setting up the dataset with the predictors:

```{r}
train_data_B<-train_data_NB[complete.cases(train_data_NB[, c("B365H", "B365D", "B365A")]),]
nrow(train_data_B)
```

Only 9 more rows were removed, which is fine given the number still left.

```{r}
selected_predictors_B<-unique(c(selected_predictors_NB, "B365H", "B365D", "B365A"))
```

and fitting the model:

```{r}
svm_model_B<-svm(FTR~., data=train_data_B[, c("FTR", selected_predictors_B)],
                 kernel="radial", cost=1, gamma=1/length(selected_predictors_B), scale=TRUE)
```

Now checking the performance:

```{r}
svm_predictions_B<-predict(svm_model_B, newdata=test_data[, selected_predictors_B, drop=FALSE])
confusion_matrix_B<-table(Actual=test_data$FTR, Predicted=svm_predictions_B)
```

```{r}
confusion_matrix_B
Accuracy_B<-sum(diag(confusion_matrix_B))/sum(confusion_matrix_B)
Accuracy_B
```
```{r}
round(diag(prop.table(confusion_matrix_B, margin=1))*100, 2)
```

This is a slight improvement for all outcomes.

```{r}
train_accuracy_NB<-sum(diag(train_confusion_matrix_NB))/sum(train_confusion_matrix_NB)

train_accuracy_NB
train_accuracy_B
```

The non-betting training data has pretty much the same accuracy for the training and test data, while the betting model seems to improve when using the test data.


**Investigating missingness for other variables**

```{r}
odds_var<-setdiff(names(train_data), selected_predictors_B)

missingness <- data.frame(
  Variable = odds_var,
  Missing_N = sapply(train_data[odds_var], function(x) sum(is.na(x))),
  Missing_Percent = sapply(
    train_data[odds_var],
    function(x) mean(is.na(x)) * 100
  )
)

missingness <- missingness[
  order(-missingness$Missing_Percent),
]
```

Checking the table:

```{r}
missingness
```

It seems that a few of the betting odds have relatively low missingness.
We will work with the 3 sites at under 12%
Imputing:

```{r}
library(mice)
```

```{r}
impute_vars <- c(
  "BWA", "BWD", "BWH",
  "WHA", "WHD", "WHH",
  "IWH", "IWD", "IWA"
)
```

```{r}
# Combining all of the predictors together: we are going to impute the missing values in the 12 rows total we had
# previously removed

selected_predictors_imputed <- unique(c(
  selected_predictors_B,
  impute_vars
))

train_imp <- train_data[
  , c("FTR", selected_predictors_imputed),
  drop = FALSE
]

```

```{r}
ini <- mice(
  train_imp,
  maxit = 0,
  printFlag = FALSE
)

meth <- ini$method
pred <- ini$predictorMatrix

meth["FTR"] <- ""

pred[, "FTR"] <- 0

for (v in selected_predictors_imputed) {
  if (anyNA(train_imp[[v]])) {
    meth[v] <- "pmm"
  } else {
    meth[v] <- ""
  }
}

imp <- mice(
  train_imp,
  method = meth,
  predictorMatrix = pred,
  m = 1,
  maxit = 5,
  seed = 123,
  printFlag = FALSE
)

train_imp_filled <- complete(imp, 1)

```

This should have imputed all of the values that were missing, let's check:

```{r}
colSums(is.na(train_imp_filled))
```

As this is good, we can once again try to build an svm model of this and we'll just check its baseline performance on the test set, but first we must check for missingness in the test set:

```{r}
colSums(is.na(test_data[, selected_predictors_imputed, drop=FALSE]))
sum(!complete.cases(test_data[, selected_predictors_imputed, drop = FALSE]))
```

Unfortunately unlike with the match statistics and Bet365 odds, there seems to be a fair amount of missingness - to be precise, (1436/8740)*100 = 16.43%. So a bit higher than the 12% cutoff from the training data, but as it's just for a baseline performance we will just impute the missing values in the test dataset as well.

```{r}
test_imp <- test_data[
  , selected_predictors_imputed,
  drop = FALSE
]

imp_test <- mice(
  test_imp,
  m = 1,
  method = "pmm",
  maxit = 5,
  seed = 123,
  printFlag = FALSE
)

test_imp_filled <- complete(imp_test, 1)
```

```{r}
# Checking that it's worked:
sum(is.na(test_imp_filled))
```

Time to fit the svm in the same way as the original models:

```{r}
# Converting result to factor again
train_imp_filled$FTR <- factor(
  train_imp_filled$FTR,
  levels = c("H", "D", "A")
)

svm_imputed <- svm(
  FTR ~ .,
  data = train_imp_filled[
    , c("FTR", selected_predictors_imputed),
    drop = FALSE
  ],
  kernel = "radial",
  cost = 1,
  gamma = 1 / length(selected_predictors_imputed),
  scale = TRUE
)
```

and test its performance:

```{r}
svm_predictions_imputed <- predict(svm_imputed, newdata = test_imp_filled)
confusion_matrix_imputed <- table(Actual = test_data$FTR, Predicted = svm_predictions_imputed)
```

```{r}
Accuracy_imputed <- sum(diag(confusion_matrix_imputed))/sum(confusion_matrix_imputed)
```

```{r}
confusion_matrix_imputed
Accuracy_imputed
```

```{r}
round(diag(prop.table(confusion_matrix_imputed, margin = 1)) * 100, 2)
```

Unfortunately as the accuracy is very slightly lower than with just the B365 odds, but still in turn reasonably higher than without any betting odds, we can reason that adding betting odds as a predictor improves predictive performance, but does not stack with more and more sites, i.e. there isn't any extra predictive power to be gleamed from multiple different sites in this experiment.

In particular, the SVM(s) had strong problems knowing when to classify a draw, though their marginal accuracy for away and especially home wins was relatively good. The accuracy reported on the test set actually ended up being higher than on the training data, so there is no evidence of over fitting. Earlier analysis of the data revealed that the lower leagues had a smaller proportion of home wins and a higher proportion of draws in comparison with the Premier League. Thus this is likely to have contributed to the increase in overall accuracy.

**Some graphs and plots**

```{r}
odds_vars <- c(
  "B365H", "B365D", "B365A",
  "BWA", "BWD", "BWH",
  "WHA", "WHD", "WHH",
  "IWH", "IWD", "IWA"
)

odds_data <- train_imp_filled[, odds_vars, drop = FALSE]

odds_correlations <- cor(
  odds_data,
  use = "pairwise.complete.obs"
)

heatmap_colours <- colorRampPalette(
  c("yellow", "orange", "red")
)(100)
```

```{r}
heatmap(
  odds_correlations,
  symm = TRUE,
  scale = "none",
  col = heatmap_colours,
  breaks = seq(-1, 1, length.out = 101),
  main = "Correlation Between Opening Odds"
)
legend("topright", legend=c("Negative (~ -1)", "Zero (~ 0)", "Positive (~ +1)"),
         fill=c("yellow", "orange", "red"), cex=0.7, bty="n")

# Just note that the color scale should be continuous but it's hard to see, i.e. orange doesn't mean exactly 0 etc.
```

This is certainly evidence that many of the betting odds are highly correlated - in particular for the same outcomes across different sites. The red patches correspond to strong positive correlation - where the same results (Home, Draw, and Away) meet for different sites. Inversely the yellow patches are where Home win meets Away win. Meanwhile, the Draw odds seem more varied; they appear to be also highly positively correlated with the Away wins but more neutral when matched with the Home wins, which is interesting. 

This suggests that there is some overlapping information between the bookmakers odds, however these correlations alone don't fully reveal each of their individual usefulness for the classification.


*ROC curve*

We will plot 3 ROC curves for the best performing SVM using the non-imputed datasets.

```{r}
library(pROC)
```

We will need to refit the best SVMs with probability=TRUE in order to plot. Luckily we know the best parameters from the K-fold CV: 

```{r}
best_svm_B_prob <- svm(
  FTR ~ .,
  data = train_data_B[
    , c("FTR", selected_predictors_B), drop = FALSE
  ],
  kernel = "radial",
  cost = best_parameters_B$cost,
  gamma = best_parameters_B$gamma,
  scale = TRUE,
  probability = TRUE
)
```

```{r}
pred_B_prob <- predict(best_svm_B_prob, newdata = test_data[, selected_predictors_B, drop = FALSE], probability = TRUE)
```

```{r}
prob_B <- attr(pred_B_prob, "probabilities")

head(prob_B)
```

```{r}
actual <- factor(test_data$FTR, levels = c("H", "D", "A"))

roc_H <- roc(actual == "H", prob_B[, "H"], quiet = TRUE)
roc_D <- roc(actual == "D", prob_B[, "D"], quiet = TRUE)
roc_A <- roc(actual == "A", prob_B[, "A"], quiet = TRUE)
macro_auc<-mean(c(auc(roc_H), auc(roc_D), auc(roc_A)))

plot(roc_H, col = "blue",
     xlim = c(1.0, 0.0),
     main = "ROC Curves - Best SVM with Betting Odds")
plot(roc_D, col = "green", add = TRUE)
plot(roc_A, col = "red", add = TRUE)

abline(a = 0, b = 1, lty = 2, col = "grey")

legend(
  "bottomright",
  legend = c(
    paste("Home win AUC:", round(auc(roc_H), 3)),
    paste("Draw AUC:", round(auc(roc_D), 3)),
    paste("Away win AUC:", round(auc(roc_A), 3)),
    paste("Macro-average AUC:", round(macro_auc, 3))
  ),
  col = c("blue", "green", "red", "white"),
  lty = 1,
  cex = 0.8
)

```

```{r}
multiclass_auc <- pROC::multiclass.roc(
  response = actual,
  predictor = prob_B
)

print(multiclass_auc)
```

```{r}
library(caret)
```

```{r}
predicted <- factor(as.character(best_svm_predictions_B), levels = c("H", "D", "A"))


results <- confusionMatrix(
  data = predicted,
  reference = actual
)

print(results)
```

Next we will plot a bar chart of feature importance to the best performing SVM:

```{r}
baseline_accuracy<-mean(pred_B_prob==actual)
set.seed(123)

importance_scores <- numeric(length(selected_predictors_B))
names(importance_scores) <- selected_predictors_B

for (variable in selected_predictors_B) {

  shuffled_test <- test_data[, selected_predictors_B, drop=FALSE]

  shuffled_test[[variable]] <- sample(
    shuffled_test[[variable]]
  )

  shuffled_predictions <- predict(
    best_svm_B_prob,
    newdata = shuffled_test
  )

  shuffled_accuracy <- mean(
    shuffled_predictions == actual
  )

  importance_scores[variable] <- baseline_accuracy - shuffled_accuracy
}


importance_scores <- sort(importance_scores, decreasing = TRUE)
```

```{r}
par(mar = c(5,9,4,2), mgp = c(4,1,0))

barplot(
  importance_scores,
  horiz = TRUE,
  las = 1,
  border = NA,
  col = "steelblue",
  main = "Permutation Importance for the Best Betting Odds SVM",
  xlab = "Decrease in test accuracy when left out",
  ylab = "Feature",
  xlim = c(-0.01, 0.08),
  xaxt = "n",
  cex.names = 0.85,
  cex.axis = 0.85,
  cex.lab = 0.95,
  cex.main = 1
)
axis(
  side = 1,
  at = seq(-0.01, 0.08, by = 0.01),
  labels = sprintf("%.2f", seq(-0.01, 0.08, by = 0.01))
)
abline(v = 0, lty = 2)
```

Next for a scatter plot of the actual outcomes comparing Home Shots on Target (HST) to Away Shots on Target (AST):

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
```

```{r}
scatter_data <- data.frame(
  HST = test_data$HST,
  AST = test_data$AST,
  Result = factor(test_data$FTR, levels = c("H", "D", "A")),
  Type = "Actual Result"
)
```

```{r}
ggplot(scatter_data, aes(x = HST, y = AST, colour = Result)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0.2, alpha = 0.45, size = 1.8) +
  geom_abline(
    slope = 1,
    intercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",

    colour = "Match result"

```

This has a diagonal line where the number of home/away shots on target are equal.
We will visually compare this to how the best SVM splits the classification between these two features:

```{r}
scatter_predicted <- data.frame(

  AST = test_data$AST,
  Result = factor(best_svm_predictions_B, levels = c("H", "D", "A")),
  Type = "SVM prediction"
)
```

```{r}

ggplot(scatter_compare, aes(x = HST, y = AST, colour = Result)) +
```

Next we will do the same for the Bet365 Home vs Away Odds:

```{r}
odds_actual <- data.frame(
  B365H = test_data$B365H,
  B365A = test_data$B365A,
  Result = factor(test_data$FTR, levels = c("H", "D", "A")),
  Type = "Actual result"
)

odds_predicted <- data.frame(
  B365H = test_data$B365H,
  B365A = test_data$B365A,
  Result = factor(as.character(best_svm_predictions_B), levels = c("H", "D", "A")),
  Type = "SVM prediction"
)

# We use the implied probabilities, which are ~ 1/Odds to get a clearer picture

odds_actual$HomeProb <- 1 / odds_actual$B365H
odds_actual$AwayProb <- 1 / odds_actual$B365A

odds_predicted$HomeProb <- 1 / odds_predicted$B365H
odds_predicted$AwayProb <- 1 / odds_predicted$B365A

odds_compare <- rbind(odds_actual, odds_predicted)

ggplot(odds_compare, aes(x = HomeProb, y = AwayProb, colour = Result)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, size = 1.5) +
  facet_wrap(~Type) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("H" = "aquamarine", "D" = "darksalmon", "A" = "deeppink3"),
    labels = c("H" = "Home win", "D" = "Draw", "A" = "Away win")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Actual vs SVM-Predicted Results by Bet365 Odds",
    x = "Bet365 home-win probability (B365H)",
    y = "Bet365 away-win probability (B365A)",
    colour = "Match result"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

```


A boxplot comparing B365D odds before kickoff between matches that actually finished in a draw and matches that didn't:

```{r}
draw_data <- data.frame(
  B365D = test_data$B365D,
  Outcome = factor(
    ifelse(test_data$FTR == "D", "Draw", "Not a draw"),
    levels = c("Not a draw", "Draw")
  )
)
```

```{r}
ggplot(draw_data, aes(x = Outcome, y = B365D, fill = Outcome)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.75, na.rm = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("Not a draw" = "brown1", "Draw" = "chartreuse")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Bet365 Draw Odds by Actual Match Outcome",
    x = "Actual match outcome",
    y = "Bet365 draw odds (B365D)"
  ) +
  coord_flip() + 
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

```

These boxplots looking broadly similar is consistent with the SVM's struggles to classify a draw. It had been hoped that the draw odds would have provided helpful information, yet we can see that the Bet365 Draw Odds alone do not largely differ between matches that were a draw and those that weren't. This doesn't give the full picture, as they could give stronger support in combination with other features - but as shown before, the match statistics alone also had a very low marginal prediction accuracy for draws, so the improvement being limited is not surprising.
